video_title_guess: NBA Playoffs: Vincent Goodwill on Wembanyama, Knicks, 76ers, Thunder, and Draft Lottery

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: Let me assure you, he has a three-year extension that is kicking in next year where he'll be making, I think, an average of 58 million dollars. He's going nowhere. He doesn't have anything to worry about on that front. But I do think for one, the fact that he was able to end the series on his feet rather than being the next game of operation where his knees are getting worked on and it's buzzing and his hip is getting worked on and it's buzzing. Like, maybe, maybe Rich, I'm old enough where I remember the game of Operation. Maybe you guys don't remember the game of Operation, you young guys, but I remember the game of Operation. And that's what Joel Embiid looked like for the better part of his career. Now to the 76ers, is Daryl Morey still going to be the guy heading up that operation? He gave Paul George a really big contract when I'm not sure he warranted that at this stage of his career. He gave Joel Embiid this extension when Embiid was, yes, coming off of an MVP, but also has been a health issue. And now you have two long-term contracts that you know you can't get off of and I'm not sure if there's any hope. So I wonder if that organization, which has Bob Myers as an advisor to the Harris Group, is going to make significant changes in the offseason or will at least entertain it because there's not a lot of hope in Philadelphia. There's a lot of ifs and maybes and those ifs and maybes only amounted to a game seven win and an impressive comeback over the Boston Celtics, but we look at that Celtics team now, that's a team full of who.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill questions Daryl Morey's long-term contract decisions for Joel Embiid and Paul George, suggesting these deals might limit the 76ers' future flexibility and that the team lacks significant hope despite a playoff win.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: I think Oklahoma City, what, what people are saying about them is, the only way this team doesn't wind up holding up the trophy, A, is if San Antonio, who has had their number this year, takes them out, or B, health catches them. Jalen Williams, J-Dub, the All-Star J-Dub, he's been out with a hamstring injury. He's only played less than 30 games this season and he's out right now. You're hoping from the standpoint of competitiveness that he gets back on the floor and that he's healthy. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, they're doing all this work against the Lakers and the presumptive MVP hasn't had one MVP-like game. They are an absolute machine right now. I'm very much looking forward to seeing the Western Conference Finals because I think Minnesota, if they get there, this will be their third straight trip. A little bit of desperation will kick in, a little bit of this Anthony Edwards will will start to kick in. I wonder if they'll, that'll be a tougher out. And San Antonio, as I mentioned before, Victor Wembanyama learns really quickly and he despises the Oklahoma City Thunder in ways that a young player should not despise another team. So I, once again, throughout the tone of our conversation, Rich, in addition to Detroit and Cleveland not liking each other, in addition to Detroit and New York hating each other, if we wound up getting that matchup, hatred is good for the NBA. Hatred sells and so does physicality. Let the boys play.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill highlights the Oklahoma City Thunder's dominant playoff run, suggesting only the San Antonio Spurs or health issues can stop them, and notes the growing rivalries and physicality are beneficial for the NBA.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: In their eight playoff wins, they have averaged a point differential of 24.5 points per game. None of these games have been competitive. They've lost two games by a total of two points and they've won these games by a total of 196. This is a generational run that the New York Knicks are playing right now. You said it, Karl-Anthony Towns in the Draymond Green sort of Arvydas Sabonis position of point forward, it's almost Golden State-esque. Like Mike Brown spent a lot of years with Steve Kerr in Golden State and he picked up on some things offensively with the cutting and the three-point shooting and it looks like it's bearing. And maybe it took a lot of things for the Knicks to get here, to change their offense in mid-season, to change it again after game three of the Atlanta series. Similar to the way that Golden State had to change how they were playing and the lineups that they were using in their first championship season with David Lee and bringing in Draymond Green and then again in the finals, going to that small death lineup against LeBron James and it yielded championships after that. You couldn't explain it, you just have to be in a desperate situation where, boom, you, in case of emergency, this is what we're going to do. I'm not saying the Knicks are going to win a championship, but I'm saying they have unlocked something that nobody could have expected. They could have obliterated the three-point record of threes in a game had that game been competitive. Instead, they had to settle for a tie at 25.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill highlights the New York Knicks' "generational run" in the playoffs, attributing their offensive explosion to mid-season adjustments and a "point forward" strategy reminiscent of the Golden State Warriors.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: Well, I know some people might be clamoring. I've seen on some of our ESPN shows, one Kendrick Perkins has been clamoring for a suspension. I don't think that's going to happen. I think honestly the best thing for Victor Wembanyama was that he was thrown out last night. I think had he not been thrown out, had that been a flagrant one, the league probably would have come back and assessed it as a flagrant two plus a suspension. When you miss the last thirty-something minutes of a playoff game, that's almost like a full game suspension already. The league doesn't want to come in and assess another one. He's not a repeat offender. I know it didn't look necessarily like the best play, but Victor Wembanyama doesn't have the history of such a thing. We know that also he's a star, you know, that plays a part in it too. But I don't think it meets the criteria of ejection plus next game suspension in game five of a hotly contested semifinal series.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill provides an insider's perspective on why Victor Wembanyama is unlikely to face further suspension, citing his ejection as sufficient punishment and his status as a star player.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: Well, Rich Eisen, do you believe that the New York Knicks will be very forthcoming about what they would say about OG Anunoby's health? If that hamstring was falling off the bone, we wouldn't know about it, right? Like that's just the way it goes with the Knicks, okay? But I do think that the nine-day, potential nine additional days of rest, the Eastern Conference Finals may not start until May 19th. That will give OG Anunoby almost two weeks to come back from this. Two years ago, during the same semifinals of the Eastern Conference, he had a similar injury on his left hamstring. He missed games two through six of that series against the Pacers, tried to come back in game seven, it did not work.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill speculates on OG Anunoby's hamstring injury, noting the Knicks' typical secrecy and comparing it to a previous injury that sidelined him for multiple playoff games, but highlights the extended rest period as a potential benefit.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: It was, it was weird. Cause, you know, Rich, this is my first year covering the Eastern Conference in full. Like the past years when I was at Yahoo Sports, I did a lot of Western Conference stuff with Stephen Curry being over there and LeBron James. I was always sent to the number one story. I've always seen these Knicks-76ers playoff series, but TV doesn't do it justice. When you're in there and Joel Embiid is at the line and he's getting booed, and Tyrese Maxey's at the line and he's getting booed, and every time a Knick does something right, the crowd just erupts. Or what's worse, Rich, 76ers fans leaving the building at some point in the third quarter. Knicks fans waving them out as if they're saying, 'Thank you for leaving this place that you've squatted for a while. We're taking this over.' And it was great that, that they had white towels because that's what exactly what it looked like with the 76ers. It looked like they waved the white towel for two consecutive games and yielding that. I think for as much as the Knicks have played well and they played excellent basketball, when you hit ten of eleven threes in the first quarter, eleven of thirteen or whatever it was, you're playing a high level of basketball. But the Philadelphia 76ers played the part of the Washington Generals for the better part of four games in this series.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill vividly describes the hostile playoff atmosphere in Philadelphia, where Knicks fans booed 76ers players and waved out departing home fans, likening the 76ers' performance to the "Washington Generals."

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: Well, I think Rich, you have to protect your player. And I think Mitch Johnson as a, this is, you know, a younger coach, he's in his early 40s. He's going to have a very long relationship with Victor Wembanyama. This is their first time going through the playoffs. And Victor is experiencing a level of physicality that, you know, he's not initiating. Rudy Gobert and Naz Reid and Julius Randle, they're putting paws on him and that's the book on him so far. So, unless you have a goon, and last I checked, there's no Charles Oakley, there's no Anthony Mason, there's no Xavier McDaniel, Rick Mahorn, Bill Laimbeer, you know, lying around anywhere that they can add to their roster, he's going to have to be the guy at this point to protect himself. I think it was more of a macro conversation that he was having yesterday, as opposed to exactly what was happening in that moment and I don't have a problem with it because what better time is there to talk about protecting your player because you know what's going to happen in the first couple of minutes of game five in San Antonio if Victor is allowed to play? The Minnesota Timberwolves are going to go at him and try to provoke him even more.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill explains Mitch Johnson's defense of Victor Wembanyama as a strategic move to protect his young star from escalating physicality in the playoffs, highlighting the lack of "enforcers" in today's NBA.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: Well, Rich, these guys are trained, media trained. They know all the cameras are going to be on them. They are trained to be frozen. Even if it's, you know, Cleveland and LeBron James, if something like that were to happen where the hometown kid knew he was going number one and knew he wanted to go to the hometown team and that's what wound up happening, you're still going to keep a straight face. No longer is going to be the day where, uh, who I can't remember the executive's name for the, uh, New York Knicks when in the, in the blue, uh, suit when Patrick Ewing was going to be announced as the New York Knicks number one draft pick in 1985, the blue lottery. That type of reaction isn't going to happen. These guys are so sophisticated. I don't think it was a mark of, 'Man, I don't want to go to Washington D.C.' because when you look at all four teams, is there a better situation than the Wizards?
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill explains that top draft prospects like AJ Dybantsa are media-trained to maintain a "frozen" demeanor during the lottery, suggesting their lack of overt emotion isn't necessarily a sign of disinterest in their drafted team.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: Yeah, I think D.C. is one of those basketball-starved places. Like we all know from a sports perspective, you just talked about Washington and how that, that whole community rallies around that football team. The Wizards have never given their franchise much to care about, short of maybe a short stint with Michael Jordan on the back end that, that didn't turn out to be much of a playoff experience. Gilbert Arenas gave them a couple of years. Like they've had splotches but they've never had anything consistent. And now you have a potential young piece, healthy, that you can build around. They've already started the rebuild process. Maybe they figure out what they're going to do with the Trae Youngs of the world and Anthony Davises and everything else. But as Detroit has shown, as other teams have shown, the days of the five-year rebuild is over. You can turn around an NBA franchise in two to three years if you get the draft right, if you get the coach right. Like as much as we talk about there's a lack of dynasties in the NBA and a lack of teams having staying power at the top, that means teams at the bottom, if you do things right, you're not going to stay at the bottom very long either.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill argues that Washington D.C. is a "basketball-starved" market ripe for a superstar to turn around the Wizards franchise, emphasizing that modern NBA rebuilds can be completed in just two to three years.

quotes.speaker: VINCENT GOODWILL
quotes.quote: The league kind of chuckles at such things because they know Chris Finch likes to work the officials in and out of the game. Like, like these guys are actual normal human beings and then when it's 48 minutes, they all turn into maniacs that are unhinged and super competitive when you consider the stakes and everything else. And Tony Brothers is not a guy who's going to take a whole lot of guff from today's coaches. It doesn't look, you know, like, like sonically correct and everything else to see a coach sort of walking, or an official walk towards a coach and look like he initiated something. But I'm sure Tony Brothers had been hearing it all night from Chris Finch and decided to say, 'Hey, I've had enough.' These things, well, luckily, you don't have the same officials for every game so the relationships don't carry over from game to game. But once again, I don't mind that at all and I don't think the league minds it either.
quotes.why_it_matters: Vincent Goodwill dismisses Chris Finch's complaints about official Tony Brothers, suggesting it's common for coaches to "work the officials" and that officials, being human, can reach a breaking point during intense playoff games.
